title: What they debate
hook: how revelation works, how binding halakha is, and how change happens

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: more in common. Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story, on five fingers. Did you find something shared underneath a difference? Now the other hand. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

An argument about an oven, in the Talmud. Rabbi Eliezer stands alone against the other sages. If I am right, he says, let this carob tree prove it, and the tree tears itself up and moves. A tree proves nothing, they answer. Let the stream prove it, and the water flows backward. Let the walls of the study hall prove it, and the walls start to lean. At last a voice from heaven: the law follows Eliezer. And Rabbi Joshua stands up and quotes Deuteronomy: it is not in heaven. The Talmud adds that God laughed and said, my children have defeated me. Today is about the questions under that story.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT AN OVEN.` → `A TREE, A STREAM, THE WALLS.` → `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: What they debate. Three questions, and then one about all three. The first: how does revelation work? The Mishnah draws a hard line here: among those it says lose their share in the world to come is the one who denies that the Torah is from heaven, in Hebrew Torah min ha-shamayim. Some Jews hold that God gave the Torah, word for word, to Moses at Sinai. Some hold that God's revelation came through human beings, over time, with human hands and voices in it. Some hold views in between. And they still read from the same kind of scroll on Shabbat morning. The second: how binding is halakha, Jewish law? For some, the law is a command, as binding today as when it was given. For others, it is a precious inheritance that guides but does not finally decide; a person weighs it with conscience and community. The third: how does change happen? When the world changes, electricity, new medicine, new roles for women, who may adjust the practice, and by what method? A recognized scholar, ruling from earlier rulings? A committee? Each community for itself? Each person? Now the question under all three: authority. Who gets to say? Remember Rabbi Joshua's verse. The commandment, Deuteronomy says, "is not in heaven." It is near, in your mouth and in your heart. Some read it the way Rabbi Joshua did: the law now lives with its human interpreters. Others read it as: it was given clearly, so it can be kept. The same verse holds both. Over the coming weeks, each movement gets its own day, in its own words. Today is just the map of the arguments.
screen: `HOW DOES REVELATION WORK?` · `HOW BINDING IS HALAKHA?` · `HOW DOES CHANGE HAPPEN?` · `WHO GETS TO SAY?` · then, large: `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about authority in your own life. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one rule you actually live by. It might come from a tradition, a parent, a doctor, a teacher, or your own conscience. Ask it the three questions gently. Where did it come from? How binding is it, for you? And if it needed to change, who would get to change it? You don't need an answer. Just notice which question felt the hardest. Then let the rule go, and sit with the breath. The bell holds the time.
What they debate. How revelation works, how binding halakha is, and how change happens: three questions, and under them, who gets to say. Today's word.
Your line: the questions. Today, when you hear an argument, about anything, try to name the question underneath it before you take a side. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: The movements of modern Judaism differ mainly over how revelation works, how binding halakha is, and who may change practice and how; each answers these questions in its own literature and its own rabbinical bodies.

original.note: Hebrew: Torah from heaven, the phrase at the center of the debate about revelation.

trapdoor: what you thought: the movements argue about everything.
what it means: they argue about a few large questions: how revelation works, how binding halakha is, how change happens.
what a scholar hears: Torah min ha-shamayim in Mishnah Sanhedrin, and the oven argument in Bava Metzia 59b, where "it is not in heaven" overrules a voice from heaven.
recall: the Yiddish way of saying rabbi

notes: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 lists those who say the Torah is not from heaven among those without a share in the world to come; the lesson softens this to 'among its hard lines'. Confirm this framing is fair.
The three positions on revelation (verbatim at Sinai; through human beings over time; in between) are deliberately unattributed to movements here; the movement days that follow attribute them.

Hook retells the oven of Akhnai (Bava Metzia 59b) in paraphrase: carob tree, stream, study-hall walls, heavenly voice, Rabbi Joshua's 'it is not in heaven', and God's 'my children have defeated me' (reported by Elijah). Distances are omitted. Day 1211 used the Hillel/Shammai 'these and these' story, so this day avoids it.

Editor: replaced the garbled 'counts among its hard lines the belief that the Torah is from heaven' with an accurate paraphrase of Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 (denying Torah from heaven costs a share in the world to come); the first note's 'softening' no longer applies.
Readings of Deuteronomy 30:12: the interpretive-authority reading follows Bava Metzia 59b; the other reading is offered as one some hold. Confirm both are fairly put.
